<a id="architecture"></a>

## Architecture

Three touches around one table. (1) HOT PATH: progress reporting and /status stop asking the whole table; a live-only query hits the partial indexes that already exist and returns in milliseconds; the historical GROUP BY survives only behind an explicit flag. (2) RETENTION: the daemon owns a bounded purge — a store function that deletes done rows older than the window in batches, and a reconciler-style sweep (boot + timer) that calls it and records a receipt in /status and the log. (3) MINT: the dedupe rule extends to failed-non-terminal rows so row 123's duplicate cannot be minted again (a partial unique index or an ON CONFLICT rewrite — if it needs a migration, that is a stop-and-ask, not a fence break). Evidence altitude: EXPLAIN-shape and retention tests with mutations, then PROD — the one-off purge o-prime runs, and the four measurements the profile report took today, re-taken.

<a id="risks"></a>

## Risks

| id | text |
| --- | --- |
| risk-1 | A caller of queue_depth that genuinely needs history (the TUI? release notes?) breaks silently when it becomes live-only — the coder greps every caller at ack and lists them |
| risk-2 | Purging in batches while the runner writes: use `DELETE … WHERE id IN (SELECT id … LIMIT N)` with a short transaction; never a single 1M-row delete on prod |
| risk-3 | The partial unique index for failed-non-terminal keys may need a migration and a backfill guard for existing duplicates — row 123's repair already removed prod's; the migration must still tolerate them |
| risk-4 | Retention default of 7 days may be too long for a 1M/day churn — measure today's growth rate and propose a default with a number |
